items.text: Today I announced that the
Government will introduce new import, sale , and supply measures for the high-power
laser pointers under health and customs legislation. The new regulations will control the
importation of these dangerous devices, and re strict their use to authorised users who
have a legitimate purpose, such as astronomers and the New Zealand Defence Force.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Why is the Government moving to control these devices?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: Powerful hand-held laser point ers are currently cheap, easy
to obtain, and can be sold or supplied with li ttle information regarding hazards and safe
use. They can cause eye injuries and skin burns, for which ACC accepts about 10 claims
a year. They can also cause temporary flash blindness, which poses a serious risk if a
person affected is a pilot or is in charge of a vehicle or equipment. The Civil Aviation
Authority reports around 100 laser strike incidents on planes each year.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: When will the new controls be introduced?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: An order under the Custom s and Excise Act 1996 and
regulations under the Health Act 1956 to c ontrol these devices are being drafted. I
expect the new controls will be in effect by the end of this year.

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: I move, That the House take note of
miscellaneous business. I have been doing a bit of travel recently—rather more than any
sane person would want to do—but it has at least given me one opportunity to look at
the political process through th e fractured lens of the La bour and Green parties, and
then to look at the reality facing New Zealand. So, without wanting to sort of caricature
it too much, the argument from the Green-Labou r side of the House is: “The country is
going nowhere. The Government does not have a plan.” OK? But let us just look at the
facts—let us just look at the underlying facts.
This country, along with Australia, is grow ing faster than any developed country in
the world, and has excellent growth prospects. This count ry has got a cost of living
increase of less than 1 percent.  That is about as low as we  have had in three decades.
And if we drill down into th e highly sensitive issue of food prices, I wonder whether
15 May 2013 General Debate 9943
members on the Opposition benches saw the figur e for the increase in food prices in the
12 months to April 2013. I wonder whether they saw what the increase was. It was
zero—actually, I am not quite correct; it was negative 0.1 percent, all right? Does that
not make the Labour Opposition look foolish for its stupid, botched strategy of trying to
eviscerate GST by removing GST from fruit an d vegetables? It was prepared to butcher
a well-constructed policy to solve a non-existent problem.
We are looking at unemployment, which is too high for the more disadvantaged
elements of our society, but the unemployment rate is half—is half—the unemployment
rate of 17 countries in the eurozone. We are looking at after-tax wages, which have
increased by 20 percent—20 percent—since 2008, which is twice the increase in the
cost of living over that time. We are looking  at mortgage interest  rates, which are the
lowest for 50 years. Sure, if you buy a house in an upper-income area of Auckland, you
will not see the full benefit of  this. But roughly 90 percent of New Zealanders who live
in their own houses are living in houses they ha ve owned for more than 2 years. If they
are paying off a $300,000 mortgage, they ar e $230 a week better off—$230 a week,
which would be over $300 in pre-tax terms. That  is what this Government is delivering
through sound, orthodox policies that are trying to fix probl ems at the root, not this
rinky-dinky stuff coming out of the Opposition.
New Zealanders are in their homes, enjoying  the benefits of a stable Government,
and crime is lower than in the last 30 year s. New Zealanders are safe in their homes
because of the policies of this Government. What does that tell  us? It tells us that this
Government is focusing on thi ngs that matter to New Zealande rs, that it is not obsessed
with its own political navel, th at we have isolated the probl ems that need fixing in this
country, and that we are laying the foundations both in the Budget tomorrow—and I am
looking forward to Mr English’s fifth Budget; it will be a gr eat Budget and it will track
the way forward for the next 12 months —and in the progress we are making on a
sustained plan called the Business Grow th Agenda, which is going to lay the
foundations for more progress of the type th at I have just outlined. This Government
knows what it is doing and it ha s a set of Ministers, back ed by strong support from our
caucus, who are focusing on the problems that  matter to this count ry. If you just comb
through some of the statements that have been made just in the last 3 days, what you get
is a picture of Ministers w ho are working to a concerted plan, know exactly what they
are doing, and are focusing on real issues.
In the social policy area, there is the deci sion to turbocharge the scheme to provide
trades training for young M āori and Pasifika people. Six hundred places were
established in 2011. We are going to turbocharge that to 3,000. The Minister of Housing
has just announced $377 million worth of new housing for 500 State houses, and, to
accommodate the larger families of toda y, another 3,000 bedrooms. This is a
Government that knows exactly what it is doing, has got a very firm plan to put that in
place, and is making great progress.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I would like to thank the
National Party’s visiting international guest speaker whom we have just heard from.
Mike Moore once said about Tim Groser that the problem with Tim Groser is he did not
get enough credit for splitting the atom. Ther e is one thing we know for sure about
tomorrow’s Budget: whatever crumbs Nationa l might decide to throw out to New
Zealanders, whatever tinkering around and robbing Peter to pay Paul that National will
do, this will be a Budget for National’s mates, not for the people of New Zealand,
because that is the record of this Government. While our economy drifts along—the
Government promised 175,000 more jobs; that is about as likely as  a Christmas card
from Steven Joyce to Judith Collins—it is focused on a narrow set of vested interests.
9944 General Debate 15 May 2013
This is never more obvious than the shameful and shabby deal done by this
Government with Skycity. It is casino po litics from the gambler-in-chief, John Key.
This deal has stunk from day one. The Aud itor-General said it was flawed, it was not
transparent, it was not even-handed. The mo ment that John Key wrote “close off the
SkyCity angle” on those papers, that is what those officials did—that is what they did.
They went into a deal that was not transparent and even-handed. Let us remember that
there were options for this. The Government did not have to go down this path to build
this convention centre, but it chose to. It chos e to do a dirty, shabby deal off the back of
problem gamblers.
When we look at that deal, there ar e 230 extra pokie machines, 40 extra gaming
tables, cashless gaming machines, more high-denomination notes, and the kicker—a 35-
year deal, a 35-year extension. If this side of the House chooses to pass laws that change
something about gambling that is included in this deal, we will have to pay for that on
behalf of taxpayers. That will be John Key’ s legacy to New Zealand. If we want to
change our own laws, we have to pay for it. That is the legacy of this Government. We
have to pay an Aussie-owned corporate if we want to change our own gambling law.
That is a shameful, shameful thing.
As the Dominion Post said, John Key’s legacy is a shrine  of misery. It also said in
the same editorial: “Every pharaoh deserves  a pyramid.” and John Key will get one.
That is what the Dominion Post said. Well, if I can mix up my metaphors, this pharaoh
has got no clothes. He has got not only naked self-interest but empty promises that were
not kept about jobs and wages and the cost of living.

items.speaker: John Key is right
items.text: there is something dying in Wellington—it is his Government. It is
his decaying Government, because there is no brighter future for New Zealanders as
wealth concentrates in the hands of the 2.5 percent who could afford shares in our
energy company. There is no brighter futu re for the 146,000 New Zealanders out of
work and out of hope. There is no future  for the 270,000 kids in poverty. The only
people who have got a brighter future under this Government are the mates and cronies
of this Government—the vested interest s who have made super-profits off power
consumers, and the corporates who get laws written for them, all at the expense of
problem gamblers.
If the Budget tomorrow were a Labour B udget from David Parker, it would be one
that changes the settings of our economy to build and create jobs and prosperity for all
New Zealand. It would build a fairer tax sy stem. It would give hard-working people a
break with cheaper power. It would invest  in regional development that protects and
supports our environment. It would be a B udget for the people from a Government that
is proud of, and has faith in, our people. Th at would be a Labour Budget. But, instead,
what we will get is a Budget from a Govern ment mired in its own scandal and focused
on deals, selling off our laws, jobs for its mates, and governing in vested interests,
running a casino economy where the house wins and the ordi nary people suffer. New
Zealanders know this and the demise of this tawdry Government has begun.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: It seems to me that it is
becoming clearer and clearer that we have two types of Opposition party in this House
now. We have the type whose members inhabit “Planet Labour”, who should know
better, actually. They have been in Government—heaven knows how they got there, but
they have been in Government—they do know what it takes to r un a country, they do
know what is involved, yet they will just say anything to ge t back in power. They know
better and they should do better, but, frankly, for them, being back in power means that
they will sell their souls and do what it takes to get there.
Then we have their friends the Greens—we have their friends the Greens. The
Greens patently have no understanding—no u nderstanding—of what it takes to run a
15 May 2013 General Debate 9945
country, no understanding of how an economy works. They patently have no idea about
how you create jobs and what you actually have to do to create opportunity and
prospects, and no idea that the path out of  poverty—the only path—is to get into work,
to create jobs, and to help pe ople into those jobs. They clear ly have no idea what they
are doing or what it takes to run a country, and that is becoming clearer by the day.
The reality is that if you want to make an actual difference to the lives of New
Zealanders, you have to do something as a Government. You cannot spend 9 years, as
Labour did, issuing reports, working out strategies, empowering working groups, and
sitting around and talking about what you mi ght do one day. You have to actually make
a difference, and that is what this Government has spent the last 4½ years doing.
Tomorrow’s fifth Budget from Bill English will be a continuation of that.
Increasingly, we have a very obvious di fference between the Government and the
parties that support the National-led G overnment, and the Opposition—the Labour-
Green Opposition. Increasingly, it is clear that what used to be a party of the centre-left
is now swinging out to a Ch ávez-style Opposition contro lled by Russel Norman and
Metiria Turei. That is the clear difference now facing New Zealand.
We have an Opposition that is totally unconcerned about the damage it does to New
Zealand—totally unconcerned. It does not care about our reputation and how it damages
it. It does not care about our  attractiveness to investment. It does not care about our
ability to create opportunities . It is all about Opposition members doing whatever they
have to do to get their hands back on the levers. They are shameless, self-serving, power
hungry, and indulgent—and that is just David Cunliffe. Labour is a party that has shown
that it is totally unfit to lead.
Meanwhile, we are getting on with it. We ar e getting on with it  every day, as we
have done since 8 November 2008, and tomorrow’s Budget will continue to do that. We
understand that to have jobs, to have opport unities, and to raise incomes, you have to
create an environment where business is able  to invest, where investment wants to put
down roots in New Zealand, and we are doing what we can to make that happen. Every
time we do—every single initiative that creates jobs—the Opposition opposes it. Every
time we come up with sensible strategies th at will mean more jobs, more opportunities
for New Zealanders here in New Zealand, an d better outcomes for our people to stay in
New Zealand, Labour and the Greens oppose it.
One of the big changes that we are looki ng to make is reforming the Resource
Management Act, not to lower environmental protections but to en sure that there is
much greater certainty and that it does not take years and years and years, and millions
and millions of dollars, to get decisions. Just  recently we have had the Statistics New
Zealand report come out. That indicated that in the last 2 years alone up to $800 million
worth of projects had been cancelled, mostly due to concerns about the uncertainty with
the process. They know what the rules are, they know what the stan dards are that they
have to meet, but there is a complete l ack of clarity and too much time and cost
involved in the process. That means less choice for New Zealanders.
Getting the Resource Management Act right is about more jobs, cheaper houses, and
more certainty for communities, and it is not about throwing moneys into the pockets of
consultants, lawyers, and planners. It is about ensuring that the system works for us and
looks after the needs of New Zealanders. We are prioritising it. This is a Government of
action. We have done more in environmen tal protection and freshwater management
than any Government has ever done. That is the difference betw een a John Key - led
Government that makes a difference and a Labour-Green Opposition that cares about
nothing but itself.

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. T ēnā tātou katoa.
Yesterday the House debated ACT’ s charter schools bill, which M āori Party members
9946 General Debate 15 May 2013
voted for. They did not speak to it—heck no. They were too embarrassed to do that.
Hell, they were not even in the House fo r it. They must have cringed when their
National and ACT Party buddies sang their praises over it, but they still voted for it.
So what is all the fuss about? It is that the M āori Party is backing charter schools
over kura kaupapa M āori. That is what the fuss is al l about. It knows what it is doing,
too, because Pete Sharples—Associate Minist er of Education with responsibility for
Māori-medium education and co-leader of the M āori Party—is supposed to be the big
daddy of kura kaupapa M āori. The M āori Party knows that Governments have starved
kura of funding and imposed rules on them th at no other school has to adhere to, yet
kura kaupapa Māori remain one of the most successful educational initiatives for M āori
by Māori of the last 100 year s. But last night the M āori Party voted with ACT to spend
massive amounts of money on charter schools  while kura kaupapa get bugger all. That
is what the fuss is all about.
Massey University professor of education John O’Neill said that early indications are
that charter schools will get more than tw ice the level of funding that mainstream
schools and kura kaupapa M āori get, Mr Bennett. It is one thing to watch the rich white
boys give their mates all the lollies, while the poor little Māori kids get by on scraps, but
it is bloody embarrassing having to watch their M āori mates cheer them on. The M āori
Party members should be ashamed about turning their backs on kura kaupapa M āori.
That is what the fuss is all about.
Māori fought long and hard to establish k ōhanga reo and kura kaupapa M āori,
because we know that making a co mmitment to Te Reo, to wh ānau, and to kaupapa
Māori is critical to providing for successful outcomes for Māori students. The kura have
proven that to be the case time and time again—and that is a quote from Mr Henare. But
will the charter schools that the M āori Party supports make those same commitments?
Hell no. Charter schools will have no accountability to wh ānau, no commitment to Te
Reo, no responsibility to Te Aho Matua, no obligation to put registered teachers in front
of our kids, and no transparency under the O fficial Information Act, and they are going
to get heaps more mone y than kura kaupapa M āori ever got. And the M āori Party
supports that? That is what the fuss is all about, Mr Bennett.
Charter schools will not have to worry about the Office of the Auditor-General,
either. Te R ūnanga o Ng āi Tahu’s submission on the bill says: “Overseas experience
shows that Charter schools are highly sus ceptible to fraud, waste and abuse ...”. Dr
Bronwyn Hayward, a political sc ientist and senior lecturer at the University of
Canterbury, referred in her submission to the problems of crony capitalism, tax evasion,
fraud, and corruption that have plagued char ter schools elsewhere. She described them
as “a naive and reckless governance model”—and the M āori Party is voting for them!
That is what the fuss is all about.
Mainstream schools are not exactly pa thways to high achievement for M āori
students, and clearly there is much to be done to change that, but that is what the
Associate Minister of Education is suppos ed to be doing—identifying and promoting
better models, not backing expensive, hi gh-risk, low-accountab ility charter school
ventures that, as 20 years of research s hows, achieve nothing th at cannot be done
without them. [Interruption] That is what the fuss is all about, Mr Henare.
The M āori Party talks about how important it is to be at the top table. Well,
tomorrow we will find out whether that is true or whether it is just a big, fat lie to keep
those members on their big, fat salaries and in their big, fat limos while delivering a big,
fat zero on M āori education. If tomorrow the M āori Party can get for kura kaupapa all
that it is giving to charter schools, if it can  get an extension in mainstream schools on
the Te Kotahitanga programme that it brags so much about, and if it can get manaaki
tauira reinstated to help all Māori students get a tertiary education, then it deserves a pat
15 May 2013 General Debate 9947
on the back. If, on the other hand, it does not achieve these things, then it will have
failed, its mantra about being at the top table will have been exposed, and its support for
charter schools will be shown up for what it really is—a plea for scraps from a
Government whose actions prove that M āori issues rank with  the Government
somewhere between nowhere and obscurity.
That is what this fuss is really all about , because our kids—all our kids—deserve the
very best in education, not the failed experi ment that charter schools have proven to be.
Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. I appreciate that the general debate is a robust debate, but I have actually got
some concerns about Mr Henare, given the amount of time he has spent yelling through
two of the three speeches we have had—almost continuously in mine and then almost
continuously in Mr Harawira’s speech.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the member for his contribution. There has been quite a lot
of interjection throughout this debate. The Hon Tau Henare has not been the only one to
raise a very loud voice.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Tēnā koe. Tomorrow we will have a Budget that shows
that National has forgotten that New Zealanders care about the environment. It will be a
Budget that shows that National has forgot ten that New Zealande rs are proud of our
country, our stunning landscapes, and our dis tinctive plants and wildlife, from the
melodic kōkako—[Interruption]—which is much more melodic than Mr Henare—to the
kauri, and that it has forgo tten that New Zealanders want our lands, our waters, and our
coasts well looked after. Th is Government has shown that  it does not care about our
environment. It has got very weak policies, like the National Policy Statement for
Freshwater Management.
This Government shows that it does not care by its attacks on one of our most
important environmental laws, the Resource Management Act. The Minister for the
Environment claims that it is not about lowe ring environmental protection. That is not
what the Parliamentary Commissioner for th e Environment has said. With the emphasis
on quick decisions rather than sound decisi ons, the Government is  reducing the ability
of local communities to have their say. With its proposals to gut the heart of the Act by
stripping out the envi ronmental criteria th at are supposed to guide decisions, it is
turning the Act into one that promotes economic development at the environment’s
expense. The Government is weakening our environmental laws so that high-impact
development projects get less scrutiny by c ouncils, get less scru tiny by the community,
and get a faster and easier ride through the resource consent process.
At the same time as it is weakening the regulatory regime, it is giving more handouts
to intensive agriculture. Tomorrow’s Budget will subsidise irrigators by an $80 million
grant to the Government’s new irrigation company, to spend on large regional water
schemes. This is despite the fact that nearly every study on water quality shows that
land-use intensification leads to water pollution. The Government is proposing to
provide further handouts to irrigators by sp ending some $400 million from the proceeds
of selling our energy companies. The Mighty River Power share deal will mean that
New Zealanders lose the dividends that th at company provided, so that dairy farmers—
and in areas like Hawke’s Bay it will be dairy farmers, because they will be the only
ones who can afford the water—can take ove r on the Ruataniwha Plains rather than
horticulture and other more varied land uses.
This will not be a Budget about sustaina ble development, because that is not a
concept that this Government understands; it will be a Budget about debt. It will be
about increasing the ecological debt on present and future generations because of this
Government’s focus on exploiting nature for short-term gains. We have seen that in
9948 General Debate 15 May 2013
Minister Joyce’s Business Growth Agenda and the regional report he put out recently.
We have got petroleum block offers in No rthland and Taranaki; minerals exploration
permits in Northland; irrigation devel opment in Hawke’s Bay, Canterbury, and the
Wairarapa; and the commercialisation of conservation land in Tasman, Nelson, and
Marlborough as the ro ute to economic nirvan a for the regions. It is a Budget that
burdens present and future generations with more water pollution, with polluted waters
and aquifers, because the Government has not  noticed that its promotion of irrigation
has a huge cost to the environment and to pe ople. In Selwyn Distri ct—the Minister for
the Environment’s own electorate, the centre of dairying, with a big Fonterra factory—
there have been dozens of problems with gastroenteritis in Darfield, and communities in
Arthur’s Pass, Springfield, Sheffield, and Ro lleston have had to or are having to boil
their water.
This is going to be a Budget that does not recognise that we need to invest in the
environment as a basis for a healthy economy and a healthy society. We have seen the
Franz Josef Development Society telling the Mi nister of Conservati on that we need to
invest in conservation because of the impor tance of conservation to the West Coast
economy, and that we need well-resourced Department of Conservation offices. Yet
what we see is the Government finding $158 million for tourism promotion but a paltry
$5 million for the Department of Conser vation, despite the protection of those
conservation assets being cen tral to the “100% Pure Ne w Zealand” brand. The Green
Party believes that we need a Budget and a Government that look after our environment
and look after all New Zealanders, not just the top 2 percent.

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: The country is looking
forward to the delivery of another Budget to morrow, Bill English’s fifth Budget, and I
am looking forward to it too. It is going to be a Budget that is built around four
principles. Firstly, it is about responsibly managing the taxpayer’s dollar. On this side of
the House we understand that the Government does not have any money of its own; it
takes it from the taxpayer. It is not an e ndless source, and if we are taking too much
from taxpayers, there is not enough for them to be able to make ends meet. That is why
this Government lowered taxes, and that is why this Government has been frugal in the
way it spends them.
The Budget is also about building a mo re competitive and productive economy.
What we know is that over nearly a decade when members opposite were in
Government the productive part of this econom y did not grow at all.  It did not grow a
single job. The Budget is about delivering bette r public services. What that party, the
Labour Party, did when it was in Government was to grow the Public Service so big that
it was like a millstone around the neck of th e New Zealand taxpayer. We are setting
about putting that right.
The Budget is about supporting the Christ church rebuild, because as the second-
biggest city in this country, th at has to be a priority. What the parties on that side of the
House have never understood is that a Budget is about jobs and growth if it is about
nothing else. What they absolutely hate is that in the last quarter unemployment fell by
6.2 percent. They hate it. They absolutely hate it.
In my electorate of Whanganui, which includes South Taranaki, we see firsthand that
this country is built on past oral farming, and the Greens ha te that. I want to ask the
Greens a question, and the question is this : how much free education, health, and
welfare would you have in this country w ithout pastoral farming and, principally,
without dairying? The answer is stuff-all. And they do not care. They do not care where
it comes from. They believe that farmers i nvolved in dairying are dirty dairyers. They
hate all that sort of stuff. They have no reci pe whatsoever to replace the income that we
15 May 2013 General Debate 9949
would lose if they had their way. In Tara naki we have got 480,000 dairy cows—in the
Taranaki province. The contribution—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Name them.

items.speaker: Hon CHESTER BORROWS
items.text: Well, I will start with Bl ossom and Elizabeth, and I
will get to your ones after that. On a single site at Whareroa we produce 2.5 percent of
this country’s gross national product. How well do you think this country would do
without a site like the Whareroa Fonterra site?
Shortly, in the next 18 months or so, Todd Energy will be drilling 41 more wells
around Taranaki, and I say “Good on them!”. Todd Energy is building a rig right now to
be able to do that. In Taranaki, for instan ce, and in Whanganui, within my electorate,
with dairying and oil and gas we add to th is country’s growth. We add money into the
taxpayers’ coffers, because, of course, thos e people are paying tax and they are paying
royalties on these things. And what does th at do? That educates our young people. It
keeps people well and healthy so that they can work, and Labour and the Greens hate it.
We know that they hate it.
If, God forbid, Labour and the Greens gain power in this country, what are they
going to do? They are going to introduce a cap ital gains tax. That is one thing they are
going to do. They are going to raise personal tax rates. They have said that they are
going to raise personal tax rate s. The hard-case thing is that  one day they believed you
are rich in this country and on the top tax rate if you are earning $60,000 a year, and the
very next day, with no explanation whatsoever, they doubled it and said: “Oh no, you’re
not rich unless you are earning  $130,000 a year, and we’ll char ge you the top tax rate
after that.”
They are going to increase the carbon tax, a nd through that they are going to make it
more expensive to do business. They are go ing to purchase generating capacity, which
will lead to higher power prices as well. Th e other answer they have, which they may
well do, is to print money. God help us if th ey ever get the opportunity to do that. Then
they are going to put up the minimum wage  to $15 an hour, so on any public holiday
any little dairy owner is going to have to earn $52.50 just to make ends meet. It is
absolutely dumb and ridiculous. Let us l ook forward to this Budget to be announced
tomorrow. Jobs and growth—that is what it is all about.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: How can the New Zealand public
be expected to believe, when such a big d eal as the Skycity deal is announced by the
Prime Minister on television on a Monda y morning, and a few minutes later the
Minister for Economic Developm ent briefs the media, who trumpet the deal, that the
very basis of that deal—the footprint on which it is being bui lt: the land and the
ownership of the land—is not  complete? The deal on pa rt of that land, which was
announced for this big project on Monday, has not been done. The land is owned by
another organisation, Television New Zealand (T VNZ), which says that it has not been
approached. If you want to look at this pict ure I have here of the new design, you will
see that a critical part of that building that is integral to its desi gn is actually owned at
the moment by another organisation. It is like signing a deal to buy a whole house from
someone who owns only a bit of it.
Skycity is not silly. It would not be si gning a deal to invest  $402 million in a new
casino, with lots of sweeteners chucked in to make it worth its while, if it was not sure
that it had the land to do it with. The Government may be sneaky, underhand, and even
downright corrupt, but it is not silly. It wants the cas ino built, and it is  not going to let
anything get in the way of that . But I took TVNZ at its word  when I was told last night
that it had not been contacted about this issue, which was backed up by its public
relations person. It was reported in the me dia yesterday that TVNZ had not been
9950 General Debate 15 May 2013
contacted about selling this land. TVNZ is sa ying that publicly. Somebody is not telling
the truth.
In February, when TVNZ appeared befo re the Commerce Committee, it insisted—
four times it insisted—that there were no di scussions with the Government or Skycity
about it getting access to or selling that land. Under intense questioning TVNZ
eventually revealed: “Oh, wait a minute, but we have engaged an architect to have a
look at the building and what the options might be for the future.” But apart from a very
brief conversation, admitted to by the chair of TVNZ, with the broadcasting Minister
some time last year in which the Minister  denied knowing anythi ng about the issue,
both the chair and the chief executive office r of TVNZ denied that they had been
approached about this issue.
Contrast this with what John Key had said  on the very day TVNZ appeared before
the select committee. He put three statemen ts on the record, saying that there were
discussions in train and that it was all going ahead. But—surprise , surprise—the very
next day he said that he was happy to accept the assurances from TVNZ that no
approach had been made. It was all very fishy. And yet we see now from the Deputy
Auditor-General’s report that Skycity had indeed been in discussions with the
Government about acquiring that land. Somebody is not being upfront. Somebody is not
telling the truth. There are tw o options here: either Skycity  knew and the Government
knew but somebody forgot to talk to TVNZ or somebody is not telling the truth.
So let us have a look at who is on the board of TVNZ. Mr Barrie Saunders—he is the
co-founder of Saunders Unsworth. He is a former editor of the National Business
Review, and guess what? His business partner, Mark Unsworth, is Skycity’s lobbyist.
Guess who else is on the board. Mr Richard Long—Mr Richard Long, who spent 2
years working as chief of staff in the Nationa l leader’s office. Both men are very cosy
with the Government. Both men are very cosy with National Ministers.
I put it to you that it is simply unthi nkable that the Government would have
announced a deal with Skycity to build a $402 million casino and convention centre,
with fanfare and huge concessions and with  it nodding and agreeing, if it had not sewn
up the land. Yet TVNZ insists that it has not  been approached. Who has shaken on this
deal? Who are the shadowy figures in the background? Who is paying for the land? Is it
Skycity or is it a sweetheart deal with the Government trading the land for a new casino
and convention centre? What say has TVNZ ha d? This is prime i nner-city land. If there
is a price being paid, who ge ts the money: TVNZ or th e Government via a special
dividend?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I once had respect for the Labour
Party. I once thought of it as a party that ha d principles and stood for what it believed
in. But I have lost that respect for the Labour Party. It is a meek group of weak
individuals who cannot put up a decent fight in this House. It has been taken over by the
Green Party. The great Labour Party of ol d is gone. The Labour Party of today is a
faceless group of factions that has been  slaughtered by the Norman invaders. The
Normans have come and they have slaughtered the Labour Party, and look at it. Look at
the policies that the Labour Party has fallen over on in the last couple of months. No. 1
is economic policy. The Normans now govern the economic policy of the Labour Party.
The Labour Party is going to print money. It is something that it does not need to do,
but it has been forced to do it because it has been told by the Green Party what to do.
The Green Party would put up the capital gains tax. Do not let any Labour member ever
say that they wanted a capital gains tax. It is a Green Party idea. The Green Party
wanted it, and the Labour Party took it on board because it has got nothing else.
15 May 2013 General Debate 9951

items.speaker: Let us talk about another issue
items.text: energy—t hat great energy issue. The Labour Party
has given up to the Green Pa rty again. The Green Party’s nationalisation idea has been
accepted by the Labour Party.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Who is Labour’s energy spokesman?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Actually, I had a look at that. It is Gareth Hughes—that great
young man from the Green Party! I had to look up who the Labour Party’s spokesperson
on energy is. Who is it?

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: I don’t know.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I do not know. I could not find it. It was Moana Mackey. Tell
me that. I have never seen her doing anything.
The next one is transport—Iain Lees-Gallo way. He has got a great future, but he has
given in to Julie Anne Genter. I do not know why. I do not know why Julie Anne
Genter has got it over Iain Lees-Galloway, but  she has. The Labour Party is giving up
on the roads of national significance. It is  saying to the people of the Waikato and

items.speaker: Hamilton
items.text: “We don’t want your votes. Don’t vote  for us. Vote for National.” And we in

items.speaker: Hamilton are going to say
items.text: “Good on them.”
But the best is yet to come. The best is yet to come because the next policy off the
rank is foreign affairs. Guess who is going to govern that?

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Who?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Kennedy Graham. Kennedy Graham is the next Minister of
Foreign Affairs under a Labour-Green Government. Kennedy Graham is going to bore
the North Koreans out of war. Kennedy Grah am will be setting up offices in Damascus
for this country. That is the next step for the Labour Party policy.
But there is more. Tell me who the Labour Party spokesperson on foreign affairs will
be. Nobody knows. Here is the next one. Who will be the Labour Party spokesperson on
agriculture? Steffan Browning has got it—Steffan Browning has it. He is going to make
everybody go back to the communes on the farms, and we are going to have these great
10-year plans that the Labour Party will fall into bed with. That is the future of the
Labour Party.
Treaty negotiations—who should we give th at to? I think Cath erine Delahunty. I
think Catherine Delahunty has served this  Parliament well—more than any Labour
Party member has—in regard to Treaty ne gotiations. The Labour Pa rty will give in to
Catherine Delahunty. Catherine Delahunty will  be setting up the Treaty negotiations
policy for the next Labour Party.
That is a shame. It is a real shame fo r that Labour Party—a Labour Party I once
thought great things about, but now I cannot see why anyone would vote for it. It is the
Green Party in drag. The Labour Party is not  the real Opposition here; the Green Party
is. That is something that is very sad for those Labour members. Look how meek and
quiet they are, and they have given up. They  have got no fight in them. They have got
nothing left in the belly. They have got nothing in the tank. They have got nothing there.
Mr Cunliffe is smiling. He is smiling because he knows that if they have got nothing in
the tank, he is next in line. The Labour Party is over. It is a good thing for New Zealand,
but it is a sad thing for those members over there. For people like Mr Little sitting there,
who had such a future in this House, it is over—it is over. The Gr een Party is the real
Opposition. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: It is always amusing when
National puts up its D-team in the general debate. “Little Nationa l-no-friends” is what
we are looking at over there. There is no John Banks, or at least not for long; there is no
Māori Party, or not for long; there is already no Mana, in more ways than one; and now
not even Aaron Gilmore can be bothe red sticking around as National’s polling
inexorably sinks towards the magic number of  39 percent. Beware two things: the first
9952 General Debate 15 May 2013
is “Bring Back Winston”, and the second, as they shudder in their twinsets and pearls—
remember this, gentlemen and ladies—is if Judith Collins is the answer, what on earth is
the question?
Today the Labour Opposition has got to note a very sad day in New Zealand politics.
It is the announcement of an extremely dodgy deal around the Skycity convention
centre. The convention centre deal is bui lt on a foundation of—and I do not use this
word lightly—dishonesty. It is dishonesty that it would not cost taxpayers a cent when
there was a multimillion-dollar slush-fund s ubsidy for Skycity in the design, and
dishonesty in the fact that the Ministry of Economic Development would not release the
records of its multiple meetings with Skycity. It was behind closed doors, just like John
Key’s meeting with the Skycity board. It was dishonesty about not hing being dodgy in
how John Key personally suspended the proper  process, which ha d four bidders, and
only Skycity got a look in. That was dishonest y in the words of the Auditor-General’s
office, which said it was “flawed” and “unfai r”, that “the SkyCity proposal was always
going to be the most attractive”, that it was not “transparent or ev en-handed.”, and that
that applied to both Ministers and officials.
It is dishonest to say that there is goi ng to be a sinking lid on pokies in Auckland,
when they have just voted for another 230 of them and 20 more gaming tables. It is
dishonest to say that the criminal ticket -in, ticket-out technology will reduce problem
gambling. The reason it is illega l is that it gives the casi no so much information about
the gamblers, so that it knows what buttons to push to get them addicted. It is dishonest
to say that there will be no cost to the country to plonk the hulking pokie palace right on
top of Television New Zealand. Who is paying  for that? It is dishonest of Peter Dunne
to feign concern, saying that the Government “did play very fast and loose at times.”
with the deal, when he holds the casting vote.  This is Peter Dunne’s palace as well as
John Key’s.
There is egregious dishonest y in claiming that Labour di d the same thing in 2001,
because it was none other than Judith Col lins who was the then chair of the Casino
Control Authority, which used a law that  National passed and Labour abolished—just
like her office—to put through the last increa se in pokie machines. There is one more
dishonesty that tops them all. It is the mother  of all rorts, and that is the dishonesty of
using Government legislation to give a go ld-plated guarantee of compensation to a
private company. That is a slippery slope in our constitution. There is dishonesty in the
numbers. As David Shearer has said, Skyc ity has hit the jackpot. By KordaMentha’s
estimates, it can make up to $530 million on a $402 million outlay. That is a 32 percent
premium for a no-risk investment, and it still owns the building at the end of the 35-year
gold-plated period.
This is a very sad day for New Zealand’ s democracy. The Government has already
sold the law on The Hobbit to Warner Bros. It has already sold the rules about spectrum
licensing to MediaWorks. Now it is selling the gambling laws about casinos to a casino.
It is giving the casino a gold-pl ated guarantee. It is selling our law. It is compromising
the sovereignty of Parliament. But I have got news for this Government: those laws that
can be made can be unmade. Any future Government can repeal the compensation
provisions and deal with the i ssues in the interests of New Zealanders, as it is required
to do. Let us be very clear. The Labour Party has no truck with the dishonesty that is on
display from this Government. We are willing to bet that neither do New Zealanders.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I would like to just commend
my colleague David Bennett for a great sp eech. I looked across the House and saw
Kevin Hague, and he smiled more than once, and I think he agreed with that speech.
Then I looked across to that side of the House and saw Davi d Cunliffe smile more than
once, and I think he agreed with that spe ech, because he knows his day will yet come.
15 May 2013 General Debate 9953
He knows that Labour is desperate, and he knows that the Greens are gleeful and that
we are seeing Labour’s desperation to find  traction with the Ne w Zealand public. We
see that it is making Labour vulnerable to the Greens’ ultra-socialistic policies.
Labour over there believes that it can enhance competitive power pricing by
becoming the monopolistic buyer of wholesale electricity in the country. It will not be a
free market any more; it will be constrained with generators and retailers brought to
their knees, and Labour loves it. It is a da ft idea, and we welcome all Labour’s daft
ideas, because it just goes to prove to New Zealand how sensible and how solid the
National-led Government really is. Colin Es piner, no friend of the Government, calls
this “Third World, funny-money stuff.” Nationalising electricity has been likened by the
New Zealand Herald to a 1930s command economy solution, not unlike what Soviet
Russia would employ. These comments are from people out there who are
commentators; they are not people who are taking political sides.
We know that Shane Jones is a political survivor, but, Shane, this is one big dead rat
that you have to swallow. We have always thought that you were smarter than the rest
of them, but it is sad to see you trying to convince yourself that this is good policy.
Shane, this is just the beginning of the dance,  and there are lots of  rats coming. This is
the classic “rearranging the deckchairs on the Titanic” policy of the Labour Party—
lower power prices and a reduced dividend to  Government. Labour will have to jack up
and rearrange taxes to compensate. Its power policy requires a taxation  increase that is
similar to the reduction in elec tricity bills. Will Labour lift ta xes? You have got it. This
is the dark cloud in its silver lining. It is redistribution of wealt h—it is plain to see.
Labour would fund the Government’s loss of dividend revenue with increased taxation
from the growth sector of the economy. That is what it is going to do.
Expect company tax to increase. Expect capital gains tax to come into play.
Businesses and farms will be paying more th rough the nose. Expect the marginal tax
rates to increase, especially for the top half of earners. Expect emissions trading scheme
increases. Labour will strip the private sect or of capital through excessive taxation and
obstructive regulation, and by necessity th e Government will become the bailout
investor in the electricity infrastructure, simply because at reduced rates of revenue
generators will not develop new generati on assets. We know that. The revenue from
those assets will not cover the costs of building them, so it is going to be the
Government that is going to bail them out. And guess what, everybody? That means
higher taxes. The final responsibility of security of supply will fall on the Government.
You would have thought that David Parker understood this after the debacle in 2008,
when, as the Minister of Energy, he was calling for 15 percent cu ts in electricity
consumption. Back then the New Zealand Herald  criticised the planning and
management of electricity supply, describing it as a maze to get through. This is the
cartoon by Mr Body. Right there in the middle, there is the maze—there is the maze of
the Labour Government’s management of electricity. The scary thing is that you will go
into that maze and you will find Trevor Mall ard in there. You will find Phil Goff in
there. You will find David Parker in there, and David Shearer in there. That is the
frightening thing. And they are all lost.
What we need to acknowledge is that 2008 was the second-driest year in the last 81
years. It was a drought time for New Zealand. [Interruption] It was a tough time, David.
But what many people do not know is that the si ngle driest year in the last 81 years was
last year, 2012, and no one knew about it. Congratulations, Mr Brownlee, on your 2010
electricity reforms. You took us through a very difficult time. National has got the
policies that will lead this country; Labour and the Greens continue to have daft ideas.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I take a call on behalf of New Zealand First,
and I ask the question: what do New Zealanders  want from the Budge t? That is the big
9954 General Debate 15 May 2013
question—what do New Zealanders want from  the Budget? Tomorrow is a critical
Budget, and New Zealanders will be watching it with interest.
New Zealanders do not want more empty phr ases and self-promoting rhetoric. They
are sick of that. Their patience is w earing thin. After 4½ years of a National
Government, they are asking themselves: “OK, after 4½ years, when are we going to get
the brighter future we were promised—when are we going to get the brighter future we
were promised?”, because they are waiting fo r it. New Zealanders are waiting for that
brighter future. They want to  see more than words. They are looking for a Budget that
will deliver real improvement in their lives. So what do they want to see?
First, they want to see a Government that actually has a plan—a Government that has
a plan. They do not want to hear comments such as thos e the Prime Minister made
about Wellington, when he said that he did not  really have any idea what to do to
improve Wellington. They do not want to hear words like that. New Zealanders want to
know that this Government has a plan. They  want to know that this Government is
capable and is not just meddling along, stumbling along, in a piecemeal fashion. They
do not want that. They want a plan and they want to know that it is a positive—
positive—outlook for the country.
But what have they been hearing from this  Government in recent times? Basically,
what they have mainly been hearing about is  deals. New Zealanders are getting tired of
just hearing about the deals. Typically, the deals are corporate deals. They are deals that
normally involve foreign interests and forei gn interests doing well out of the deals put
forward by this Government.
Kiwis deserve more than a Government that  survives just by doi ng deals with the
likes of Warner Bros, China Southern Airlines—allowing visas for high-rolling Chinese
gamblers to come to this country—Mighty River Power, and the list goes on. Kiwis do
not want to see these sorts of deals going on in this country. The Skycity deal is just the
latest example of how easily the public interest is traded off in a back-room deal. That
deal will create enormous social harm, a cost  this country will have to bear for the next
35 years.
So tomorrow Bill English must present a plan—a real plan with numbers, with times,
and with targets. That plan must addr ess unemployment, which is running at
unacceptable levels.
Simon O’Connor: It’s dropping.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: They keep saying that it is down 6.2 percent, but out in the
provinces in the areas where it is really, really affecting everyday New Zealanders, such
as in Northland—where it is 10 percent on average, but for young Northlanders it is
significantly higher than that—that is where it is really hurting Ne w Zealanders. It is
hurting young M āori and young Pacific Islanders —young people who simply do not
have work, cannot get work, and see no futu re. They see their only future as being
somewhere other than in New Zealand.
Right now there are 150,000 people who are unemployed. What we do not see is the
other, similar figure of underemployed peopl e in this country. Pe ople who have only 1
hour or more of work a week are classified  as having a job. But many of these people
would like to work a lot longer, a lot more, and would like to actually have a decent job,
but if they have more than 1 hour a week, they are not cl assified as being unemployed.
But they certainly are underemployed. In many cases, they are on the minimum wage
and are not doing particularly well at all.
This Budget must deliver jobs, particularly  for the younger workers. It must deliver
on things such as electricity. The Government does assert that the electricity system is
efficient, but back in the real world Kiwis are struggling with the cost of power bills.
The elderly are struggling with the cost of power bills. So in tomorrow’s Budget, let us
15 May 2013 General Debate 9955
hope this Government does something about the cost of power. Let us also hope that it
does something about the fact that there ar e 40,000 fewer manufacturing jobs in this
country since this Government came to  power—40,000 fewer manufacturing jobs. Let
us hope it does something about that, beca use we have New Zealanders who are
talented and enterprising, and we have the c limate and the resources in this country. Let
us hope that this Government puts somethi ng on the table tomorrow with a proper plan,
and not just cuts, cuts, cuts, and more cuts.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): It has been intere sting, as we have
listened across the House to the Opposition, th at we are blaming the Chinese, as I think
we just heard at the start of Mr Williams’ speech. We have had people make accusations
and impugning, if you wish, the reputations of  people who sit on boards. We have had
people jumping up and down about  how we dare allow a busi ness to actually build a
convention centre in the city of  Auckland that will bring jo bs and opportunity. It is an
incredible amount of negativity.
But I want to talk around a different asp ect today. As many of you will know, I have
spent an awful lot of time in university—fortunately, most of it while also working.
Because of those years in uni versity, I have become an advocate of lifelong learning,
and I am thrilled to be in Parliament, a pl ace where so much learning is possible. From
the National Party you can learn all about  good government and sensible economic
management. From the Labour Party, well, you can learn how a green tail can wag a red
dog. From the Green Party itself, well, look, my stars—to use a quote—the things you
can learn from the Green Party. Maybe we in this House sometimes take for granted the
fascinating things that the Green Party says , given how often we hear from it, so I
thought we would just reminisce a little.
We hear from Dr Russel Norman. He has de livered some extraordinary lectures on
“Harry Potter economics”. From what I unders tand, his theory is that most economic
problems can be solved with the judicious us e of magic. With a wave of his wand he
can create money out of thin air. I have learnt from him that quantitative easing is a way
to make photocopying money seem like an economic policy.
But he does not just make money appear. He  can make money disappear as well. For
example, he and David Shearer, the “deput y leader of the Green Party”, made $500
million disappear from the New Zealand st ock exchange overnight—overnight—with
only a few words. They made $500 million disappear from or dinary Kiwis’ savings in
the likes of KiwiSaver and the New Zeal and Superannuation Fund. It was an amazing
magical feat. But, you see, Dr Russel No rman has also found a way to make power
prices disappear. His plan is to nationalise the energy sector, following in the footsteps
of such great economic luminaries as Ma rx, Lenin, and Mao. Yes, Dr Norman never
fails to delight when pulling rabbits out of his hat.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: Out of his what?
SIMON O’CONNOR: Out of his hat.
But he is not the only Green Party member  to have graduated from the “Hogwash
School of Witchcraft and Wizardry”. It sounds like Metiria Turei is fa irly similar, with
puffs of smoke as well. You see, “Professor Tu rei” has taught all of  us about enterprise
and initiative with her small-business programm e. It is entitled, if  I read the lecture
notes correctly, “Growing the economy by growing marijuan a”. This past April she
actually said, and I am quoting, that “There’s some real sk ills [in growing the drug] …
some real entrepreneurial skills, some real horticulture skills …”. I understand that in
the next semester “Professor Turei” will be teaching graduates of those classes
advanced chemistry, in a course called “P labs : our path to prosperity”. Yes, children—
you listening in—the Green Party believes that you too can grow up to be a drug dealer.
9956 General Debate 15 May 2013
Sometimes when I listen to the lectures the Greens put forward, I am not entirely
convinced—I am not entirely convinced. But learning is about being exposed to new
ideas, and so I have listened. The word that comes to mind when I listen to the Greens is
“ideology”. There are few political partie s around the world as committed to their
ideology as the Greens are. In the face of all the facts, desp ite all the evidence that says
that their extremism will not work in the real world, the Greens stick to their ideology.
And do you know what? You have to kind of admire that sort of dogged commitment. It
reminded me of the lost Japanese soldiers in the 1970s who refused to accept that World
War II was over. Like them, the Greens refuse to surrender to logic, to reason, and to
progress. So I say “Soldier on.” to the Gr een Party educators. Bestow your wisdom on
this House, let nothing sta nd in your way, and the Labour Pa rty will be right there to
support you to do whatever you tell it to do. I cannot wait to see what the Greens will
teach us next.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

sections.heading: Prohibition Of Gang Insignia In Government Premises Bill

items.text: Second Reading

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: I move, That the Prohibition of Gang
Insignia in Government Premises Bill be now read a second time . The bill restricts the
display of gang insignia in central government and local government premises. It makes
the display of gang insignia in government  premises an offence and empowers the
police to arrest the person who wears it and to seize the offending article. I would like to
thank the chair and members of the Law and Order Committee for their work on the bill
and for the amendments they have recomm ended to include every school and police
building and their grounds and premises in New Zealand in the scope of this legislation.
Gangs are a scourge on society. Every politic al party in this Parliament recognises
this. Gangs commit crime, peddle poisonous drugs to our children, and create victims in
vulnerable communities. The gang patch is not  a patriotic flag or a symbol of honour
and respect; it is a symbol of intimidation by gang members who wear it. It announces
to the world that they engage in criminal behaviour and that they are proud to intimidate
law-abiding citizens.
The select committee heard from submitters  throughout the country. I want to touch
briefly on some of the submissions th e committee heard, and I do hope members
opposite will listen. The Murupa ra Area School made the forcef ul point that children at
school do not need to be exposed to gang insi gnia: “they need to be protected from it.”
Ōpōtiki District Council said that the bill  sets the right bounda ry to reduce gang
intimidation of our communities. Whakat āne District Council to ld the committee that
the bill will help reduce levels of inti midation of the public. The Whitireia Community
Law Centre, in Kris Faafoi’s electorate of Mana, spoke courageously about the chilling
effects of gang violence and in timidation in Porirua. It ha s been at the coalface of
protecting victims of crime from gang harassm ent. It said that members of the public
have a right to visit Government premises without fear.
I call on Mr Faafoi, who received that submission in the committee, to listen to his
own community, which is telling him to suppor t this bill. You see, the Labour Party has
said that it does not think the bill is necessary. Phil Goff talked boldly in the dying days
of the last Government about banning gangs , but when it comes to supporting measures
to do something important, Labour’s voice falls short. Phil Goff and Kris Faafoi sat on
the select committee. They heard the submi ssions from the Kawerau District Council,
which said: “A legislated ban will not only protect frontline staff and customers from
15 May 2013 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 9957
the intimidation ... but will also prevent intimidation of ... staff who may otherwise have
initiated and/or had to enforce such bans case by case.”
It is wrong to put the onus on Work and In come case officers or a school teacher to
issue a trespass notice to individual members of the Mongrel Mob after they walk into a
public building. We need to rec ognise the gang patch for what it  is. It is an intention to
intimidate. A blanket ban that criminalises  this intimidating behaviour protects our
hard-working public officials, as well as the citizens who use our public services.
I call on the Labour Party to put aside this rhetoric and listen to the evidence that was
presented to the select committee. I call on it to get back in touch with the people on the
front line. They deal with the consequen ces of gang violence, gang intimidation in
vulnerable communities, and gang recruitment of young people. These communities are
asking us to introduce these measures.
Across the world, from Britain to the Unite d States to Australia, legislators are
acknowledging the problems that gangs create and are empowering their law
enforcement agencies to take action against them. Just last month Prime Minister Julia
Gillard announced across the Tasman plans to crack down on gangs. Some of these
measures, including the confiscation of pro ceeds of criminal gang activity, are already
available in New Zealand. Australia realises the threats that gangs pose to society and,
unlike other parties in this Parliament here in New Zealand, is prepared to take action.
Over the past 4½ years, putting the intere sts of victims of crime and law-abiding
citizens first has been the guiding principle of this Government’s law and order policy.
We have increased sentences for our wors t offenders. We have improved victims’
rights. We have put 600 more police on to th e front line. We have made it harder for
offenders to get bail. We are giving the police the technology to spend more time on the
beat and less time at their desks. Police patrols are up by 70 percent. We have improved
technology to intercept gang communications  and we have the powers to dismantle
gang fortifications. These policies are successful, because we are now seeing the lowest
levels of crime for some 24 years. Violent crime has dropped by 17 percent in the last 4
years, after steadily increasing under the previous Government.
There is not much about the Mongrel Mob that my electorate of Rotorua is proud of,
but we were proud that the fi rst ever seizure of assets under the Criminal Proceeds
(Recovery) Act involved th e Mongrel Mob in Maket ū. Valentine Barclay Nicholas, the
local chapter boss who had violent criminal convictions going back some 30 years, had
all of his beachfront property seized. Nine cars and his treasured Harley-Davidson were
confiscated from him. Just a few weeks ago, we announced the seizure of $150 million
from criminals since the Government passed this very important legislation. For the first
time ever, gangs are starting to hurt, and it is because we are arming our enforcement
agencies with the right tools.
At the same time we must be aware that gangs will change and adapt. There are
indications that gangs are becoming more sophisticated in their transportation and
manufacture of drugs, and in how they transf er assets, how they intimidate people, and
how they communicate with each other. But criminals are not always very smart. The
police are now using their powers effectiv ely to intercept co mmunications between
gang members—their phone calls, their text messages, and their emails can now be
intercepted. For those criminal masterminds who freely parade their gang patches on the
internet, it is not just their Facebook frie nds who now know what they are up to. As a
Parliament we cannot stop t echnology, but we must be vi gilant about how gangs are
using technology and we must support the fi ne work the police do by giving them the
tools to respond to this. We must constantly update these tools.
This bill will make it harder for gangs to intimidate New Zealanders. It is not a silver
bullet to ban gangs in New Zealand, but it is another important tool to make law-abiding
9958 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 15 May 2013
New Zealanders feel safe in their communities. I look forward to the House supporting
this bill through to the Committee stage. Thank you.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: I would like to thank the member for Rotorua
for laying down that challenge to listen to  the Whitireia Community Law Centre, which
is a very good law centre in Porirua, and a la w centre that I respect a lot. But I am not
going to meet that challenge. I am going to throw another challenge back to the member
here: if he really cares about what the Whitireia Community Law Centre thinks about
intimidation in our community of Porirua,  he should go and put a decent piece of
legislation in this House that would actually  be effective in doing something about the
intimidation by gangs in our communities.
Do not bring this window-dressing piece of legislation, the Prohibition of Gang
Insignia in Government Premises Bill, through to this House. Do not come into this
House and challenge me about my constituents  and a law centre th at I have a duty to,
and say that this bill is going to do something about it, because it is not. It is not going
to make one bit of difference to gang intimidation in our communities. So, Mr McClay,
if you want to come to Porirua, let us go and see the Whitireia Community Law Centre.
Withdraw this bill from the House, and let us  put something in front of this Parliament
that is actually going to deal effectivel y with the issue of gang insignias and gang
intimidation in our communities. If you are truthful about it, let us go and do that, and
let us put a piece of decent legislation in front of this House.
It is funny, because the most passionate part of  this bill that has come back from the
Law and Order Committee actually comes fr om the Labour Party. We actually say:
“Labour has no truck with gangs with a culture that promotes, encourages, facilitates, or
tolerates criminal activity collectively or individually among its members.” Well, that is
100 percent right. The member who just t ook his seat, Todd McCl ay, was right. No
party in this House has any tolerance for gangs, the intimidation that they do play in our
communities, the criminal activ ity that they organise and carry out, and the grief that
they create in our families and communities. But, as I said before, this bill goes nowhere
near effectively dealing with the problem of gangs in our communities. It fails to deal
with the substantial problem. It fails on the test of being clear a nd consistent to deal
with gang problems and the questions of w hy people are joining gangs and why they
commit crime. This bill does little or nothing.
It does succeed in a few things, though. It succeeds in terms of the illusion of
tackling crime, which is one of the things th at the National Party definitely wants to do.
It succeeds in terms of maximum exposure for tr ying to look like it is doing something,
with minimum effort—with minimum effort. It certainly succeeds in the National Party
looking like it is doing somethi ng or being tough on somethi ng where there is going to
be no practical difference.
This bill adds nothing to the powers that al ready exist, and that certainly is the point
in case in my electorate of Mana. The memb er said that the select committee added
police stations on to the list of Government premises that are covered under this bill. Mr
McClay, I will take you out to Porirua right now and I will show you at the entrance to
the police station, where it says: “No gang patches allowed in this station.” The police
are already taking action to make sure ther e are no gang patches on their premises, so
why do we need to bring this in? The legislation already exists—the legislation already
exists—to make sure that any intimidatory behaviour is policed.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: The police love it. They think it’s fantastic.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: But the problem here is that it is not being enforced. It is interesting
that the Minister of Police is piping up, because the police, who are under huge pressure
because of the budget cuts that this Govern ment has brought in, cannot police things
like this—they cannot police things like this. So the police Minister might want to think
15 May 2013 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 9959
about why they have to bring in this piece of legislation and about  the ability of the
police to enforce the current laws.
I would have to say that the stretched police resources—we heard yesterday Radio
New Zealand saying that there are 213 fewer front-line police staff on the front line
right now than there were in June last ye ar. The police Minister can say whatever she
likes over here—but that is a Government that said it was going to get tough on law and
order and beef up police numbers—but we know that there are 213 fewer police because
of the budget pressure that this  Government has put the poli ce under. It is an absolute
fact. The numbers coming from the police Mi nister’s own office, own department, are
that there are fewer police officers on the fr ont line. In black and white, this is a
Government that says it backs police, but it does not, because there are fewer police
officers on our front line at the moment.
What is more, because of the budget pressure  that the Government has put the police
under, there are fewer police trainees going through the Police College.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: Rubbish.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: There are.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Table them now.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: I will table the written parlia mentary questions I get from—
roughly, I think, in 2011 there were 450 trai nees going through the Royal New Zealand
Police College, then last year it was roughly 265. So half the number of police trainees
went through the Police College in the previous year.
Let us look at the Ten One  magazines at the mome nt. If you look at the Ten One
magazines at the moment, at the back of the magazine it starts li sting who has left the
police force. I am sure the police officers who are in this House will see—Mark
Mitchell will be watching that closely, and Chester Borrows—that a lot of their mates
whom they know through long-time policing are starting to resign. The numbers are
starting to creep up. So what is going on with the police at the moment when
experienced officers like Grant Coward out of  New Plymouth are saying: “OK, I have
had enough of this place; I’m out of here.”? He had 20 years of policing experience, and
this Government is letting experienced polic e officers go, all because that Minister is
starting to cut the budgets.
The truth hurts; the truth hurts that Government. That is exactly what the truth is. Our
police are stretched, and this is one of the pl ethora of things that they can no longer
manage to keep an eye on. So why is the G overnment making these cuts, and why is it
bringing in this window-dressing piece of le gislation? Nothing good is going to come
out of this piece of legislation.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: The Minister’s agitated. You’ve got her good.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: She is—the truth hurts, unfortunate ly. Let me go back to the bill.
Let me go back to the bill, because I did want to acknowledge some of the submitters,
and the one that Mr McClay did mention, b ecause I think they did make a very good
submission. That was the Murupara Area School. It did make two points why it
supported the bill. The first on e was that children and stude nts did not want to see gang
insignias plastered around their school and that  they needed to be protected from them,
and also that the introduction of gang insignia into the school’s premises: “would create
tensions and unnecessary negative behaviour and we want to discourage that type of
behaviour from our school.”

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: It was a good submission.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: It was a good submission. I will say that. It was a good submission.
But the message that we sent to that school at the time, in terms of the Opposition
members, was that there are laws already in place—

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: You weren’t there when they came in.
9960 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 15 May 2013

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: I beg your pardon?

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: Were you there when they came in?

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: I was there—were you there?

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: Yes, I was there.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: OK, good. We were both there. Thanks for establishing that—
thanks for establishing that. I was there. I listened to it. I actually knew one of the
submitters. So—

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: You weren’t there when I submitted.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Just pipe down for a second. It was a very good submission in the
fact that we said to the submitters that there are already laws that exist to make sure that
their concerns are already catered for. This bill certainly does not do anything new, and
will not be effective in making sure that the threat of gang intimidation will be stamped
out in our communities.
There are also a number of anomalies in th is bill about who can do what and where.
One of them is that you can wear a gang patch on Government premises, but that does
not apply to things that could also be consid ered offensive, like a swastika. I think that
is a strange anomaly in this bill. I think most people would wonder why you can not get
away with a gang patch, but something highly offensive, like a swastika, is not captured
in the bill.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: Put a Supplementary Order Paper, Kris.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Maybe we will put in a Supplementary Order Paper. We will
probably put a few Supplementary Order Papers in, to get rid of most of the things in
this bill.
There was also another anomaly—that you could be wearing a gang patch on a
covered footpath that is operated by a c ouncil or owned by the Government, and that
was a no-go area for anyone who was wearing a gang patch, but you could certainly be
on an uncovered footpath and you would be fine  being there. Another anomaly is that
you could be at a bus station or a train stat ion, and that could be a covered building or
premises, but then if you were in an uncovere d bus station or train station, well, that
would be a go area. So there are holes in th is piece of legislation, right through it, that
mean that we on this side of the House cannot support it.
What the Government should do is take a good look at a decent pi ece of legislation,
look at what some of the factors are, and at the reason why some of these youngsters are
joining gangs—factors like youth unemployment, which is at a high level. Maybe, just
for the benefit of the Minister of Police, the Government should look at some of the
harm that her budget cuts have done to the po lice and are causing some of the issues, so
that the laws that are currently in place are not being enforced. If this Government talks
tough on law and order, it should back it up wi th a budget and some legislation to do
that, but it has not.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: We have just had to endure a 10-minute
speech from Kris Faafoi, and only 2 minutes of  it was devoted to the bill at hand, the
Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government  Premises, because I believe that Todd
McClay, the author of this most excellent bi ll, has touched a really raw nerve with Mr
Kris Faafoi. He is beside himself becau se he knows that the submission from the
Whitireia Community Law Centre is absolutely right. This bill is making a huge
contribution to tackling the problem of gangs  in New Zealand. Mr Kris Faafoi knows it,
and we have this submission from the law centre that absolutely backs this bill and
backs Todd McClay’s position. It has utterly destroyed the reputation of Kris Faafoi in
his electorate, and he is very, very worried—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Not hard to do.
15 May 2013 Prohibition of Gang Insignia in Government Premises Bill 9961

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: That is not hard to do. He is ve ry worried about that because Kris
Faafoi knows that anything that  this Parliament can do to tackle the gang problem in
New Zealand is a good thing.
The bill has been widely supported by the submitters who came to the Law and
Order Committee, and it will do its bit to tackle the scourge of gangs in his electorate.
That is what is biting and eating away at Kris Faafoi so much—he knows that that is the
truth. Kris Faafoi knows that there will be people out there in Porirua, his electorate,
who are looking at this debate today and w ho will be absolutely dismayed at the fact
that their member of Parliament, who is mean t to be representing their interests in this
place and who should be supporting this bill, is finding himself in a policy no-man’s
land where he is forced to espouse a position th at in his heart he does not believe. In his
heart he knows that it will be eroding the pop ularity that he enjoys  a little bit of in
Porirua, his electorate.
The Whitireia Community Law Centre said some things to us that were very
compelling and were in support of Todd McClay ’s bill. It had this to say, by way of a
submission to us: “In the early 1970’s, the Mongrel Mob moved into the Porirua Area
and since then they have had a strong presen ce in our community.” You see, these are
people who really care about their commun ity. “With high unemployment, increased
availability to drugs and a rise in poverty the Mongrel Mob offers an alternative to
young men who are often estranged from th eir families, products of broken homes
and/or had long associations with Child Youth and Family.”
So this law centre cares about and repres ents vulnerable people in Kris Faafoi’s
constituency. They are the ones who care a bout the constituenc y. They are supporting
the bill. Why is Kris Faafoi not  supporting a bill that does ju st a bit to help tackle the
gang problem in New Zealand, which this Government is so focused on doing? In his 8-
minute rant about the New Zealand police what  Kris Faafoi did not  say was that crime
is dropping in New Zealand. Kris Faafoi ignor ed the inconvenient truth that there are
more police on the streets in New Zealand and in Porirua, and that crime is dropping in
his own constituency. What is eating him up so much about Todd McClay’s excellent
bill is that he knows it is th e right thing to do, but he ca nnot do a damn thing about it
because he is being told to oppose it, for ideologically bereft reasons.
Labour members can find no real reason to opp ose this bill, except that maybe, when
somebody walks along an open walkway they are not covered by the bill, but when they
are in an enclosed walkway they are cove red. Well, come on! What kind of logic is
that? I mean, we are going to hear that kind of logic from Phil Goff and that is not going
to be very convincing. So poor old Kris F aafoi has found himself having to oppose this
bill against the wishes of his own community. Man, it must suck to be him.
